name: Evidence Extraction Tables
title: Evidence Extraction Tables
answer: Evidence extraction tables are the structured grids that turn individual research reports into comparable rows and columns for a literature review or evidence synthesis. They typically capture citation details, study design, population, setting, intervention or exposure, comparator, outcomes, time points, effect estimates, and risk of bias. In AI research the same tables may also record model, dataset, task, metric, baseline, compute, and code or data availability. On this site the practice sits alongside a library of 288 research papers and 13,608 extracted claims, where each claim is meant to be traceable to its source. The table is not the synthesis itself, but the evidence base from which synthesis, meta-analysis, or narrative summary is built.

sections.body: Evidence extraction tables are the structured grids that turn individual research reports into comparable rows and columns for a literature review or evidence synthesis. They typically capture citation details, study design, population, setting, intervention or exposure, comparator, outcomes, time points, effect estimates, and risk of bias. In AI research the same tables may also record model, dataset, task, metric, baseline, compute, and code or data availability. On this site the practice sits alongside a library of 288 research papers and 13,608 extracted claims, where each claim is meant to be traceable to its source. The table is not the synthesis itself, but the evidence base from which synthesis, meta-analysis, or narrative summary is built.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Evidence extraction tables run on ordinary productivity software, relational databases, or dedicated systematic review platforms. Spreadsheets such as Excel or Google Sheets are common because they are flexible and familiar, though they can become fragile as rows and columns grow. Relational databases and review platforms offer controlled vocabularies, validation rules, user roles, and audit logs. Reference managers supply citation metadata, and statistical software or scripting languages handle the downstream analysis. Version control, cloud storage, and backup routines keep the table recoverable when multiple reviewers work on it over months.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work begins with a protocol and a data dictionary that define every field, allowed value, and unit before extraction starts. Reviewers pilot the form on a small set of studies, compare results, and revise ambiguous fields. Extraction is then done independently in duplicate where resources allow, with disagreements resolved by consensus or a third reviewer. Each value is tied to a page, section, table, or quotation in the source paper, and entries are checked for transcription errors. For AI literature, reviewers may also extract model details, dataset splits, evaluation metrics, and whether code or data are available, and the table is updated as new studies appear with changes logged so the review can be reproduced.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk in evidence extraction tables center on copyright, licensing, database rights, and the handling of personal data from human subjects. Review teams record the provenance of every extracted value, including who extracted it, when, from which version of the paper, and under what license. On this site, extracted claims link to the original paper rather than to a search tool, which keeps provenance anchored to the source. Conflicts of interest, funding sources, and study limitations are often captured as fields because they affect how evidence is weighed. Risks include transcription errors, misclassification, duplicate publication, selective reporting, and loss of context when a number is copied without its definition, so audit trails, version history, and correction logs are the usual safeguards.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward more automation, with natural language processing and large language models assisting the identification and extraction of fields from full text. Human reviewers remain in the loop for calibration, adjudication, and quality control, because extraction errors can propagate into every downstream summary. Structured data standards and shared schemas aim to make tables interoperable across reviews and reusable in living evidence products. Open extraction datasets and detailed provenance records are increasingly part of the reproducibility package. The unresolved questions are how to measure extraction accuracy, how to represent uncertainty, and how to keep automated tables faithful to the source paper.
